evals.prompt: Define a prototype as this skill uses the term, in 2-3 sentences. What makes it different from an early version of the product?
expected_elements: A prototype is an artifact built to answer a specific, written-down question — an instrument, not a draft of the product
Built at the lowest fidelity that can credibly answer that question
Disposable by design — its value is the learning, not the artifact
Distinct from an early product version, which is meant to become / ship as the real thing

evals.prompt: What is 'fidelity matching' and why is choosing the lowest sufficient fidelity the core judgment in prototyping?
expected_elements: Fidelity matching = choosing the lowest fidelity that can credibly answer the learning question
Names the ladder (paper → wireframe → clickable → wizard-of-oz → role-play → service prototype → code spike)
Higher fidelity than needed wastes time
Higher fidelity prematurely anchors stakeholders on visual decisions

evals.prompt: Why does the skill argue against polishing a prototype before showing it? What does polish cost?
expected_elements: Polish signals finality
Polish makes stakeholders evaluate fit-and-finish instead of the concept
Polish makes users reluctant to criticize; a rougher prototype invites honest reaction
The substitution effect ('a prototype is worth a thousand meetings') only holds if the prototype is cheap enough to build several and discard most

evals.prompt: A team wants to test whether users will trust an AI-suggested product category before any engine exists. Recommend a fidelity and approach, and explain why.
expected_elements: Recommend a wizard-of-oz prototype — a human secretly performs the function the system will later automate
Lets the team test trust/behavior before building the engine
Start from the written learning question (will users trust the suggestion?) and the evidence that answers it
Avoids building the real recommendation engine just to test the trust question

evals.prompt: A designer proposes a two-week high-fidelity Figma build to test whether a new onboarding flow is understandable. Critique the plan.
expected_elements: Flow-understandability is answerable at low fidelity (paper sketch or rough wireframe)
Two weeks of high fidelity is over-building — construction time should be small relative to the cost of being wrong
High fidelity anchors stakeholders on visuals and risks the prototype becoming the product
Write the learning question first and pick the lowest fidelity that answers it

evals.prompt: A teammate asks the prototyping skill to build a reusable dashboard-widget component to add to the design system. Is that in scope? Why or why not?
expected_elements: Not in scope — durable, reusable, ship-ready components are design-module-composition
Prototyping produces disposable artifacts for learning; different lifecycle, quality bar, and audience
Correctly redirects to design-module-composition rather than building a production component

evals.prompt: A stakeholder says 'a prototype is just an early version of the product, so make it as polished as we can.' Correct the mental model.
expected_elements: A prototype is an instrument for a written question, not an early product version
Build at the lowest fidelity that answers the question; it is meant to be thrown away
Judging by visual quality inverts the value system — judge by what was learned
A rough prototype that produces a clear answer (even a negative one) beats a polished one that gets defended and anchors stakeholders

evals.prompt: Before and after building a prototype, what would you check to verify it was done well?
expected_elements: There is a written learning question agreed before construction, plus a definition of what evidence answers it
Fidelity matches the learning goal and the team can defend the choice
The prototype is disposable in the team's mind — no implicit commitment it becomes production; construction time small vs the cost of being wrong
It is testable by a real participant and there is a written plan for after testing (iterate / escalate fidelity / kill)
